newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says N. Korea will not make meeting.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says N. Korea will not make meeting.

text.p: North Korea on Friday told the United States it will not make an important meeting set for Feb. 5 in New York, raising grave doubts about the future of proposed peace talks on the Korean peninsula.

"We were informed late this afternoon by the (North Korean) U.N. Mission in New York that the North Korean side would not depart Pyongyang in time to attend the joint briefing scheduled for February 5 in New York," State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said in a written statement.

He said, however, that the North Koreans "have not informed us that they are unwilling to attend such a meeting" and the Americans "will be in touch with the North Koreans seeking further clarification."
Pyongyang had already delayed the briefing once because of inconclusive talks with Minneapolis-based Cargill Inc. over a grain deal for North Korea.
The briefing, organised by the United States and South Korea, was to consider a proposal for four-way peace talks concerning the Korean peninsula that would also include China.
Washington and Seoul proposed the four-way talks last year.

"We are disapppointed at this latest turn of events but the U.S. and ROK (Republic of Korea or South Korea) briefing to the DPRK (Democratic People's Republic of Korea or North Korea) on the proposal remains valid," Burns said.
"We hope to move ahead with the joint briefing at the earliest opportunity," he added.

The briefing was originally set for last Wednesday but Pyongyang, seeking a barter deal for 500,000 metric tons of grain with U.S. grain trader Cargill Inc, asked that the meeting be delayed until Feb. 5.

"Latest reports are that unless North Korea receives more grain or gets grain for the Cargill deal...they have no intention of going to the briefing," U.S. ambassador to South Korea James Laney told a news conference earlier in Seoul.
"That puts a great deal of doubt on the four-party talks."
A State Department official in Washington said North Korean diplomats had not shown up in Beijing to get their visas from the United States Embassy. The United States has no embassy in Pyongyang.

North Korea, following months of resistance, agreed in December to attend the crucial U.S.-South Korean briefing after negotiations with Washington that led to a Pyongyang apology for a September submarine incursion into the South.
The negotiations paved the way for Cargill to receive a permit from Washington to barter grain for North Korean minerals.
The shipment is crucial for Pyongyang, which is suffering an acute food shortage after severe floods in 1995 and 1996.

But Laney said no deal had yet been struck between Cargill and Pyongyang. "As yet, Cargill has not found a sufficient basis for that barter. The United States government of course has nothing to do with private business," he said.
Burns said the United States had no immediate plans to make a direct food shipment to North Korea.
He also denied news reports that the United States and North Korea had agreed to set up liaison offices in each other's capitals by July.
"We've not agreed to any specific date for it. There are still some logistical issues that need to be worked out," Burns told a news briefing.

The two countries agreed in principle in October 1994 to set up liaison offices. The United States has sent a diplomat, Evans Revere, to South Korea to learn Korean so that he can take over the U.S. office in Pyongyang when it opens.
